answer.exemplar: Virtual memory lets each process be given its own address space, so the program can be written as though it had the whole machine and two programs cannot scribble on each other, and it lets more processes stay resident than RAM alone would allow by keeping cold pages on disk. The benefit stops where the working set stops fitting: past that point almost every reference is a fault, the system spends its time moving pages rather than running them, and throughput falls below what it would have been with a smaller program. That is why the system degrades sharply rather than gently, and why adding a second program to a full machine can make both slower.

answer.exemplar: Parity is redundancy inside the array: it reconstructs a single lost drive from the data still on the array, which makes the array tolerant of failure, not protected from loss. It shares a fate with what it protects, so a controller that writes wrong data, a filesystem that corrupts a file, malware, or an accidental deletion all leave the array perfectly self-consistent, and parity will faithfully reconstruct the wrong data or nothing at all. A backup is a copy at a different place on different media with its own retention, and it can only answer the question parity cannot: what the data was before the damage. Adequate evidence would name a restore that has actually been performed from an off-array copy, with the time it took and what came back, since an untested backup is a claim rather than a copy.

questions.explanation: If one block took every update to a hot file it would be erased far more often than its neighbours and would wear out alone, so the controller remaps updated blocks to whichever free cells have the fewest erase cycles, which spreads the wear and lets the drive fail across its whole life rather than in one place. Keeping the speed even is a genuine benefit of a controller and not the reason for the mechanism, because the cost of erasing does not depend on which cell is erased. Remapping says nothing about recoverability or about reserving space for a log, and a drive that wrote everything to a few cells would simply have a shorter life.

answer.exemplar: Replay works because the log is written ahead of the medium, so every acknowledged write is recoverable in principle, and 9,600 entries at 1,500 a second is 6.4 seconds of catch-up, which tells you the system recovers and roughly how long the recovery window is. What it does not establish is that the data is correct: replay restores what was accepted, not what was intended, so a write acknowledged with wrong contents, or an ordering the medium had already partly applied, is faithfully reproduced as it was. It also does not close the window, because those same 6.4 seconds are when a second failure leaves both the log and the medium inconsistent. Adequate evidence would pair the replay time with a verification of the recovered records and a statement of what happens if the log itself is lost.

questions.explanation: A 32-bit address field gives 2^32 sectors, and at 512 bytes each that is 2^41 bytes, which is 2 TiB, so 8 TB minus 2 TiB leaves 6 TB unaddressable. Dividing by 2^40 instead of 2^41 treats the sectors as 1024 bytes each and gives 8 TB minus 4 TiB, which is 4, and dividing by 2^30 treats them as 512 billion and gives nothing. The 2 TiB reachable is a hard ceiling set by the address field rather than by the drive, which is why the same drive behaves differently on a wider interface.

answer.exemplar: The two figures measure different things rather than contradicting each other: the burst figure holds only while the on-board cache can serve the request, and it falls to the sustained figure once the read has to come off the medium, which on a drive drawing real power is also where heat and current limits begin to bite. Nothing is dishonest in quoting both, since a short benchmark genuinely does reach the higher number, and a reviewer who compares the two without asking how long each holds has settled the answer before reading the sheet. The trap is using the burst figure to size a job that reads more than the cache holds: 20,480,000,000 bytes at 3,000 MB/s is 10.24 s and at 1,800 MB/s is 14.63 s, so a 43 percent optimism becomes a missed window. Adequate practice is to size on the sustained figure and treat the burst figure as describing a cache hit rather than the device.
